newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bank of France trims intervention rate to 3.25 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bank of France trims intervention rate to 3.25 pct.

text.p: The Bank of France trimmed a key interest rate on Thursday in an apparent sign of its approval of the conservative government's 1997 budget.
The Bank said it was lowering its intervention rate to 3.25 percent from 3.35 percent at a money market tender.
The Bank left the five-to-10 day rate, which is considered less important at the moment, unchanged at 4.75 percent.
"It is a validation of the budget," Credit Lyonnais economist Valerie Asselot said.
"It means the Bank of France did not see the budget as being a threat in terms of inflation or the franc," Societe Generale economist Michala Marcussen said.

Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said that France's low inflation had permitted the rate cut. He told LCI television that the interest rate was currently "extremely low" and at the lowest level for more than half a century.

He also said the rate cut had been possible because of regained confidence in the franc in the foreign exchange markets and the governments commitment that it will bring the state deficit to three percent of GDP in 1997.

"The first reason ... is that we have a very good result inflation wise. The previous month (July) we hade a 2.3 percent rise in prices, we have now (August) 1.7 percent. We are fully in line with our strategy which was, for the monetary council, to say that the price rises needed to be less than two percent at the end of the year," he said.
On Wednesday the government unveiled a 1997 budget which lowered spending in real terms and allowed France to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on European monetary union.
But the government had to resort to exceptional revenues, such as a payment from France Telecom to cover pension liabilities in the years ahead, to meet its goal.

Economists had been split on whether the Bank would cut interest rates on Thursday, with some saying they expected the Bank to wait for the dust to settle after the budget, especially given a slight weakening in the franc against the mark.
The franc was trading at 3.4063 per mark shortly after the rate cut, lower than before the budget announcement but off the low of 3.4092 it reached on Wednesday.

In cutting the intervention rate, the Bank of France narrowed the premium of French official rates over German rates which had widened after the Bundesbank cut its repo rate to 3.00 percent from 3.30 percent on August 22.

At the time the Bank of France cut only 20 basis points off the intervention rate. The French central bank usually holds the intervention rate just above the German repo rate to cushion the franc against any currency attack.
"They did not follow the Bundesbank entirely (after the last cut) and now they have cashed in on that," Marcussen said.
Economists said the Bank of France still had room to trim the intervention rate further, though only by a small amount.
"By only catching up with the Bundesbank they've signalled they're being cautious. They could have done more and been OK," Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International, said.
"It's not terribly unexpected but what it does do is suggest there's scope for rates to come down further," she said.
